title: Pythagoras' three questions
hookLine: the Golden Verses: where did I slip, what did I do, what did I leave undone? (Golden Verses 40–44)

cards: You know Pythagoras from school. The triangle. A squared plus b squared.
What school usually leaves out: around 500 BCE, Pythagoras also led a community in southern Italy that was half math club, half spiritual order.
His followers kept rules about food, silence and friendship, and believed the soul lives many lives. And they had an evening habit that Sextius and Seneca would inherit, centuries later.
It survives in a short old poem, the Golden Verses, and it asks three questions before sleep.

teach.b: The Golden Verses are about seventy lines of advice, credited to Pythagoras but almost certainly written down by his followers much later. Nobody knows exactly when; scholars' guesses range over several centuries.
Near the middle comes the evening practice. In paraphrase: don't let sleep close your eyes until you've gone over each thing you did today, three times. Where did I go wrong?
What did I do? What that I ought to have done did I leave undone? If you've done badly, the poem says, be troubled by it; if well, be glad.
Put these beside Sextius's questions from two days ago and you'll see a family likeness, and one real difference.

teach.h: WHERE DID I SLIP? WHAT DID I DO?
teach.b: Sextius asked about improvement: what did I cure, where am I better.
The Golden Verses ask something harder to see: what did I leave undone? Most reviews only catch the things you did. The sharp word.
The late email. But a day is also made of what you didn't do. The friend you meant to call.
The thank-you that stayed in your head. The walk you skipped. Those make no noise, so they never show up at 1am.
The third question goes looking for them on purpose.
The habit traveled: Epictetus quotes these same lines to his students in the Discourses, and tells them to use the verses in daily life, not just recite them.

teach.h: THE THINGS THAT MAKE NO NOISE.
teach.b: Three questions, from a community most people remember only for a triangle.

how: People drawn to ancient philosophy sometimes use the Golden Verses' three questions as an evening review: where did I go wrong, what did I do, what did I leave undone.

games.q: you've reviewed the sharp words and late emails of your day. the Golden Verses have one more question. what is it?
games.why: what did I leave undone. the things we didn't do make no noise, so the third question goes looking for them.

practice: Run the three questions over the last day: find one moment where you slipped, even a little, then one where you did well, and let yourself be glad about it.
Then ask slowly, what did I leave undone, and let something quiet surface, a message, a kindness, a small promise. Don't fix it now; just notice it.

orig.note: Greek, from the Golden Verses: where did I go wrong? literally, where did I step aside from the path?
